title: Our ears: hearing sounds from near and far

summary.text: Shut your eyes, and you can still tell if Amma is calling from the next room or from right beside you. Your ears catch sounds from every side, near and far. The ear flap catches a sound, and it goes down the ear hole to the eardrum inside. A sound gets softer as it travels further away. Your child tests if their ears can tell near from far, and may find that a soft sound close by can sound far away.
summary.art: A girl sitting on a chair with a dupatta over her eyes, smiling, while her mother stands a few steps behind her holding a steel tumbler and a spoon.

intro.hook: Close your eyes. Somebody says your name. Without looking, can you point to them? Can you tell if they are near or far?
intro.text: Your eyes are shut, yet you know where the voice is. Your ears found out. Ears catch sounds from in front, from the sides and even from behind you. In this unit you look at your ears, listen for near and far sounds, and test if your ears can be tricked.
intro.art: A boy with his eyes closed and one arm pointing behind him, while his grandmother, standing behind him, calls his name with a smile.

outcomes: By the end I can point to my ear flap and ear hole, and say that the eardrum is inside, at the end of the ear hole.
By the end I can say that a sound gets softer as it travels further away.
By the end I can say how I guess if a sound is near or far, and that a soft sound close by can trick me.
By the end I can say how one other animal hears in their own way.
By the end I can keep my ears safe: cover them for very loud sounds, and never put anything inside them.
By the end I can make a guess, test it fairly, and say what I found out.

terms.meaning: Hearing is the sense that tells you about sounds. Your ears are the sense organs for hearing.
terms.example: You hear the pressure cooker whistle from the next room.
terms.art: A child standing in a doorway with a hand at one ear, and a pressure cooker on a stove in the kitchen beyond, with curved lines of sound coming from it.

terms.meaning: The ear flap is the part of your ear you can see and touch. Its folds catch sound and send it into the ear hole.
terms.example: When you cup your hand behind your ear flap, a soft sound gets a little louder.
terms.art: A close drawing of a child's ear, with the curly folds of the ear flap shaded and an arrow pointing into the ear hole.

terms.meaning: The eardrum is a thin skin at the end of the ear hole, deep inside your head. It is stretched tight, like the top of a drum. When sound reaches it, it shakes very slightly.
terms.example: You cannot see your eardrum, but a doctor can, with a small torch.
terms.art: A doctor looking into a girl's ear with a small torch, and a round picture beside them showing the tunnel of the ear hole with a thin round skin at its end.

terms.meaning: A loud sound is a big sound, like a drum close by. A soft sound is a small sound, like a whisper.
terms.example: A temple bell is loud next to you, and soft from three streets away.
terms.art: Two pictures side by side: a child holding their ears next to a big drum, and a child leaning in to hear a friend whisper.

explanations.definition: Your ears are your sense organs for hearing. The ear flap catches sound and sends it down the ear hole to the eardrum inside.
explanations.description: The part of your ear you can see is the ear flap. Its curly folds catch sound and guide it into the ear hole. The ear hole is a short tunnel into your head. At its end is the eardrum, a thin skin stretched tight. When sound reaches it, the eardrum shakes very slightly. Deeper inside, your ear turns that shaking into messages for your brain. Then you hear. You have two ears, one on each side of your head. So you hear sounds from in front, from the sides, and from behind you.
examples: Cover your ears with your hands, and sounds go quieter. Less sound can get in.
Cup your hand behind your ear flap, and a soft sound gets a little louder. Your hand catches more sound, like a bigger ear flap.
Your ear hole makes a little wax. The wax keeps the tunnel clean and moves out by itself. Never put a cotton bud, a pencil or anything else inside your ear.
explanations.context: This card shows the parts of your ear and what each part does.
explanations.art: A friendly drawing of a child's head from the side, with labels on the ear flap and the ear hole, and a round zoom picture showing the tunnel and the eardrum at its end.

explanations.concept: Sounds get softer as they travel further
explanations.definition: A sound spreads out all around from where it is made. The further it travels, the softer it gets.
explanations.description: When a spoon hits a steel tumbler, the sound spreads out on every side at once. Close to the tumbler, a lot of that sound reaches your ear. Far away, the same sound has spread over a much bigger space. So only a little of it reaches you, and it sounds soft. Walls, doors and curtains also soak up some sound on the way. That is why a vegetable seller is loud at your gate, and soft from the end of the street.
examples: A flower seller calls 'Mallepoolu!' at the gate. As she walks away down the street, her call gets softer and softer.
An auto horn right next to you makes you jump. The same horn three streets away is just a small beep.
In the Find the Hidden Song activity, the song got louder as you came closer to the phone.
explanations.context: This card says why far sounds are soft.
explanations.art: A woman walking down a street with a basket of jasmine on her head, calling out, and curved lines around her that are big and bold near a child at the gate and small and faint at the far end of the street.

explanations.concept: How you tell if a sound is near or far
explanations.definition: Your ears hear how loud a sound is. Your brain uses that, and what it already knows, to guess how far away the sound is.
explanations.description: A loud sound usually means near, and a soft sound usually means far. Most of the time that guess is right. But it can be tricked. A soft tap close by can sound far away. A hard tap across the room can sound near. Your brain also uses what it knows. You know how loud a friend's voice usually is, so a very quiet friend sounds far. Echoes help too. A far sound reaches you with more echo from the walls.
examples: In the Near or Far test, the trick taps often fooled your ears.
Thunder is very loud, yet it is made high up in the clouds, far away.
A mosquito is very soft, yet when you hear one, it is right by your ear.
explanations.context: This card explains what you found in the Near or Far test, where you guessed with your eyes shut.
explanations.art: A girl with covered eyes on a chair, with two small pictures: a grown-up close behind her making a tiny tink on a tumbler, and a grown-up far away by the door making a big ting.

explanations.concept: Every animal hears in their own way
explanations.description: Humans and other animals hear, but not all in the same way. An elephant hears very low rumbles from her family, from far away. A female cricket hears with ears on her front legs, and walks towards a male's song. A frog's eardrums are on the outside, as round circles behind the eyes. A snake has no ear flaps and no ear holes. Snakes pick up the shaking of the ground through their jaw. Plants may hear too. Every animal who listens hears the world in her own way. Scientists agree that all these animals hear. They argue about whether plants hear.
examples: In 1984, Katy Payne found that elephants call each other with rumbles too low for people to hear.
In 2019, Lilach Hadany and her team played the buzz of a bee to evening primrose flowers. Within a few minutes, the flowers made their nectar sweeter.
A street dog lifts and turns her ears towards a sound before you have even heard it.

perspectives.explanation: The evening primrose flowers heard the bee and got ready for her. Hearing is any way of sensing sound, and these flowers do that in their own way.
The flower test is a good start, but it needs to be done again by other teams. They would call it a response to sound, and keep the word 'hearing' for beings with ears.

explanations.context: This card is about how other living beings hear. Scientists still argue about whether plants hear.
explanations.art: Four small scenes: an elephant with ears spread wide, a cricket with a tiny ear circle on her front leg, a green frog with a round eardrum behind the eye, and a yellow evening primrose flower with a bee buzzing near.

agreed.text: We hear when sound goes into our ears.
agreed.evidence: Cover your ears tightly and sounds go quiet. Doctors have looked inside ears and found the eardrum and the parts behind it.

agreed.text: A sound gets softer the further it travels.
agreed.evidence: Walk away from a ringing phone, and it gets softer with every step. Scientists have measured this many times with sound meters.

agreed.text: Babies hear before they are born.
agreed.evidence: In 1980, Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer showed that babies only a few days old already prefer their mother's voice. They had heard it from inside her body.

challenging.claim: A loud sound is always close by.
challenging.who: A guess many children and grown-ups make
challenging.for: Most of the time, the closer you are to a sound, the louder it is.
challenging.against: Thunder is very loud, yet it is made far away in the clouds. A whisper right by your ear is soft. How loud a sound is depends on how big the sound is, as well as how far away it is.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that loud always means near.

challenging.claim: Cotton buds are a good way to clean inside your ears.
challenging.who: A common habit in many homes
challenging.for: Ear wax looks like dirt, so people want to take it out.
challenging.against: Ear wax keeps the ear hole clean and moves out by itself. A cotton bud can push wax deeper, or hurt the eardrum. Doctors say to wipe only the outside of the ear.
challenging.context: This card is about cleaning ears.

challenging.claim: Elephants have huge ears so that they can hear far-away sounds.
challenging.for: A big ear flap can catch more sound, as your cupped hand does. Elephants do hear their family from far away.
challenging.against: Elephants flap their huge ears to cool down. Their ears are full of blood vessels that lose heat in the breeze. Some scientists think elephants also feel low rumbles through their feet.
challenging.context: This card is about why elephants have such big ears.

big_questions.q: Arjun whispered right behind Meena, and she thought he was far away. Was the mistake in the room, or in Meena's guess?
big_questions.hint: Arjun was close. The 'far away' was Meena's guess. Where does a guess happen?

big_questions.q: You can shut your eyes and still know where a voice is. What do you know with your ears, and what do you only guess?
big_questions.hint: Think about the soft tap close by that sounded far away.

big_questions.q: An elephant hears her family from far away, where you would hear nothing. Is the elephant's world bigger than yours?
big_questions.hint: Think about all the sounds the elephant hears that you do not. Do you hear some that she does not?

big_questions.q: If you could hear any sound in the world, from as far away as you like, which would you choose?
big_questions.hint: A friend in another city, the sea, a whale, the inside of a seed, your own heart?

story.title: Who Is Calling Meena?
story.note: Hyderabad is a city in Telangana. 'Nanamma' means father's mother in Telugu. 'Mallepoolu' means jasmine flowers in Telugu. A koel is a bird whose loud call is heard all over India in summer. Meena, Arjun and Nanamma are made up.
text: Meena was six. She lived on the fourth floor of a tall block of flats in Hyderabad. She lived with her Amma, her little brother Arjun and her grandmother. Meena called her grandmother Nanamma.
One summer evening, the power went off. The fan stopped. The flat went dark and very still.
'Come,' said Nanamma. 'Let's sit on the balcony and play my listening game.'
They sat on the cool floor of the balcony. 'Close your eyes,' said Nanamma. 'Tell me every sound you hear. Then tell me if it is near or far.'
Meena shut her eyes tight. At first she heard nothing at all. Then the sounds came, one after another.
'Ku-oo! Ku-oo!' 'A koel,' said Meena. 'He is near. He must be in our neem tree.' 'Good,' said Nanamma.
Then came a long, low 'Paaam'. 'A train,' said Meena. 'Far away, at the station.'
'How do you know it is far?' asked Nanamma.
Meena thought. 'Because it is soft. A train is very loud when you stand close to it.'
A pressure cooker whistled. 'Next door,' said Meena. 'Near.' Down in the street, a woman called, 'Mallepoolu! Mallepoolu!' 'The jasmine seller,' said Meena. 'Down at the gate. Far, but not very far.'
Nanamma smiled in the dark. 'Your ears are working hard,' she said. 'They catch sounds from near and from far. And you have two of them, so they catch sounds from every side, even from behind you.'
Arjun was four, and he did not like sitting still. Very quietly, he crept away.
Then Meena heard a tiny voice. 'Meena,' it whispered. 'Meeena.'
'Someone is calling me from the street!' said Meena. 'Far away, down by the gate.'
Nanamma began to laugh. 'Open your eyes,' she said.
Meena opened them. Arjun was standing right behind her. He had both hands over his mouth, and he was giggling.
'You were right here!' said Meena. 'But you sounded so far away.'
'He whispered,' said Nanamma. 'A whisper is a soft sound. Your ears heard a soft sound, and you guessed that it was far away. Most of the time that guess is right. Tonight it was wrong.'
Meena frowned. 'So my ears can be tricked?'
'Everyone can be tricked,' said Nanamma. 'Me too. Let's try.'
So Nanamma shut her eyes. Meena whispered 'Nanamma' right next to her. Then Arjun ran to the far end of the corridor and shouted 'Nanamma!' as loud as he could.
'The whisper came from far away, and the shout from close by,' guessed Nanamma. Then she opened her eyes, saw where they really were, and laughed. 'You tricked me!'
Just then, there was a deep rumble, far away. Arjun grabbed Meena's arm. 'That was very loud,' he said. 'Is it near?'
'That is thunder,' said Nanamma. 'Thunder is made high up in the clouds. It is so loud that you can hear it from very far away. Loud does not always mean near.'
Soon the rain came. Fat drops drummed on the balcony rail, very near. The koel stopped calling. Far away, the train called once more.
That night in bed, Meena listened in the dark. The rain was soft now. Then, very close, someone whispered, 'Goodnight, Meena.'
This time, Meena was not tricked. She reached out her hand, and there was Arjun, right beside her.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Meena finds that her ears tell her how loud a sound is, and that she guesses near or far from that. Arjun's whisper from close by fooled her, just as the trick taps in the Near or Far test can fool your child. The thunder shows the other trick: a loud sound can be far away.
ask: How did Meena know the train was far away?
Arjun was right behind Meena. Why did she think he was down at the gate?
The thunder was very loud. Was it near?
At the end, how did Meena find out where Arjun really was?
art: A girl and her grandmother sitting on the floor of a dark balcony in a Hyderabad flat, eyes closed, with a koel in a neem tree beside the balcony.
A small boy creeping up behind the girl on the balcony, whispering, while the grandmother watches and smiles.
The girl opening her eyes in surprise to find her little brother giggling right behind her.
Rain falling on a balcony rail at night, with a flash of lightning far away over the city.

games.title: Near, Middle, Far: hop to where the sound is
games.players: 1 or more players and one caller. With 2 people, one is the caller and one hops. With more, take turns to hop.
games.context: This is a moving game. Three big cards on the floor say NEAR, MIDDLE and FAR. The caller reads a sound card, and the player hops to where that sound would be.

printables.title: 3 big floor cards
items: MIDDLE: in the next room or at the door
FAR: down the street or up in the sky

items.f: A mosquito buzzing by your ear
items.b: Near. A mosquito is soft, so if you hear one, it is very close.
Far. Thunder is made high in the clouds. It is so loud you hear it from far away.
Near. It is right above you.
Far. Aeroplanes fly very high, but they are very loud.

items.f: Someone stirring a pot in the kitchen of the next flat

items.b: Far. Train horns are loud, so you hear them from far away.
Near. A whisper is soft, so your friend must be close.

items.f: A koel calling in a tree outside
items.b: Middle or far. A koel is loud, so the bird can be quite far.

img.credit: Tom Heijnen, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: The doorbell of your own flat
A drum band in a festival procession in the street
items.b: Far or middle. Drums are loud, so you hear them from far down the street.

items.f: A ticking clock on your table
items.b: Near. A tick is soft, so you hear it only close by.

items.f: A pressure cooker whistle next door
A ship's horn at the harbour, heard from a beach far away
items.b: Far. Ship horns are made very loud so that they carry far.

rules: Put the three floor cards in a line, a big step apart. NEAR is closest to the player.
The caller mixes the 14 sound cards and reads the front of one out loud.
The player hops to NEAR, MIDDLE or FAR, and says why.
The caller reads the back. If the player's reason makes sense, the player gets a point, even if the card is not the one on the back.
Play 7 cards, then swap jobs and play the other 7. With 4 players, one is the caller and the others hop in turn, one card each. Add up the points together and try to beat them next time.
A child who cannot read yet can be the caller if a grown-up reads each card quietly to them first.

setup.art: Three large paper cards on a floor in a line, marked NEAR, MIDDLE and FAR, with a child standing at the NEAR end ready to hop.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the three floor cards in a line.

setup.art: A child landing on the FAR card while a woman reads a sound card out loud.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the sound card, then hop to where that sound would be.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three floor cards in a line. 2. Stand your child at the NEAR end.
flow.say: These cards say near, middle and far. When I read a sound, hop to where that sound would be.
flow.kid: Look at the three cards. Near, middle, far. Get ready to hop.

flow.do: 1. Mix the sound cards. 2. Read one at a time. 3. Your child hops and says why. 4. Read the back. 5. After 7 cards, swap: your child reads and you hop.
flow.say: Thunder in a storm. Is thunder near, middle or far? Hop! Why did you choose that one?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Hop to near, middle or far. Say why.

ask.q: Thunder is very loud. Why is it on FAR?
good: Because it is up in the clouds.
It is loud, but it is far away.
Thunder is so big that we hear it from far.

flow.parent: Some cards have more than one good answer. Praise any reason that makes sense, like 'a koel is loud, so she could be far'.

flow.do: Ask the check question. Then add up the points together.
flow.say: How many points did we get? Let's try to get more next time.
flow.kid: Count the points. Can you win more next time?

check.q: You hear a mosquito buzzing. Where is the mosquito?
check.why: A mosquito makes a very soft sound. You hear it only when the mosquito is very close, often right by your ear.

games.title: Window Sound Bingo
games.players: 1 or more players, each with a bingo board.
games.context: This is a listening game at a window or a balcony. You listen for nine everyday sounds. When you hear one, you cross it off and mark it N for near or F for far.

printables.title: A bingo board of 9 sounds, in 3 rows of 3

rules: Each player sits by the window or on the balcony with a board and a crayon. With 2 people, you can share one board and play together.
When you hear a sound on your board, cross it off. Write N in the square if it was near, or F if it was far.
The first player to cross off a whole row says 'Bingo!' quietly. Keep listening, because other rows can still be won.
After 8 minutes, stop. If nobody got a whole row, the player with most squares crossed off wins. A shared board is a shared win.
Count your N and F marks. A grown-up reads the squares to a player who cannot read yet.

setup.art: A child sitting by an open window of a flat with a crayon and a paper board of nine squares, each with a sound written in it.
setup.caption: 1. Sit by the window with your bingo board.

setup.art: The same board with three squares crossed out in a row, an N written in one and an F in two.
setup.caption: 2. Cross off each sound you hear, and mark N or F.

flow.do: 1. Sit by a window or on the balcony. 2. Give each player a board and a crayon. 3. Read the nine squares together.
flow.say: We are going to listen for these nine sounds. When you hear one, cross it off. Then write N for near or F for far.
flow.kid: Look at your board. Listen for these sounds. Cross off each one you hear.

flow.do: 1. Everyone listens quietly. 2. Help your child mark each sound N or F. 3. Ask how they knew.
flow.say: You crossed off the horn. Was it near or far? How did you know?
flow.kid: Cross off a sound. Was it near or far? Write N or F.

ask.q: How did you know the horn was far?
good: It was soft.
It came from the road down there.
It sounded small.

flow.parent: In a flat, many sounds come from the street below or the flats around you. Some sounds are hard to place. That is fine. Ask your child for their best guess and their reason.

flow.do: Count the N and F marks together. Ask the check question.
flow.say: How many near sounds did you hear? How many far ones? Which was the farthest sound?
flow.kid: Count your N marks and your F marks. Which was the farthest sound?

check.q: The same scooter horn sounds loud, then softer and softer. What is the scooter doing?
check.why: A sound gets softer as it travels further. If the horn gets softer and softer, the scooter is going further away.

experiments.title: Near or Far? Can your ears tell with your eyes shut?
experiments.context: In this experiment you sit on a chair with your eyes covered. A grown-up hits a steel tumbler with a spoon, from close by or from across the room. You guess near or far. Then come the trick rounds.
experiments.question: With your eyes shut, can your ears tell if a sound is near or far? Can a soft sound close by trick you?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With your eyes covered, will you always know if the tumbler is near or far? Could a soft tap close by trick you? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You sit in the same chair every round, with your eyes covered. The grown-up uses the same tumbler and the same spoon. The grown-up moves only while you cover your ears and count, so footsteps do not give the place away. Which spot comes next is decided by the paper chits, so you cannot guess a pattern.
results_table: Where the grown-up was: near or far

materials.item: a dupatta or soft cloth to cover the eyes, or just closed eyes
6 small paper chits, made by a grown-up
paper and a pencil for the results

experiments.safety: Never hit the tumbler right next to anyone's ear. The near spot is one big step behind the chair, not at the ear.

schedule.what: Guess, then do 3 normal rounds and 3 trick rounds of near or far, then talk about what fooled you.

experiments.record: Draw yourself on the chair. Draw the near spot and the far spot. Put a tick for each round you got right, and a cross for each round that tricked you.

setup.art: A chair in the middle of a living room, a small chalk cross one big step behind it marked NEAR, and another cross by the far doorway marked FAR.
setup.caption: 1. Put a chair in the room. Mark a near spot and a far spot.

setup.art: A girl on the chair with a dupatta over her eyes and her hands over her ears, counting out loud, while her mother tiptoes to the far doorway with a tumbler and spoon.
setup.caption: 2. Cover your ears and count while the grown-up moves.

setup.art: The girl with her hands down, listening, as her mother gently hits the tumbler with the spoon, with small curved sound lines.
setup.caption: 3. Listen to the tap. Say near or far.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan and the TV. 2. Put a chair in the middle of the room. 3. Mark a near spot one big step behind the chair. 4. Mark a far spot across the room, by the door. 5. Make 6 chits.
flow.say: We are going to test your ears. You will sit here with your eyes covered. I will hit this tumbler with a spoon, sometimes near and sometimes far.
flow.kid: Sit on the chair. Look at the near spot and the far spot.
flow.parent: Write the chits secretly. The three normal chits say 'normal near', 'normal far' and 'normal near'. The three trick chits say 'soft near', 'hard far' and 'soft near'. Keep the normal chits in one pile and the trick chits in another, and mix each pile.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess. Write their guess down.
flow.say: With your eyes covered, will you always know if I am near or far? Could I trick you? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Will your ears always know near or far? Why?

good: Yes, because near sounds are loud.
No, because I can't see you.
Maybe, if you hit it softly.

flow.parent: Any guess is fine. Do not say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Cover your child's eyes. 2. Pick a normal chit. 3. Your child covers their ears and counts to ten out loud. 4. Walk quietly to the spot. 5. After the count, hit the tumbler once, the same way each time. 6. Write the guess. Do all three normal chits.
flow.say: Cover your ears and count to ten, out loud. Now hands down. Listen. Was that near or far?
flow.kid: Cover your ears. Count to ten. Hands down. Listen. Near or far?

ask.q: Near or far? How did you know?
good: Near, because it was loud.
Far, because it was soft and small.

flow.parent: A normal tap is a medium hit. Most children get these right. Do not say if a guess is right until the end.

flow.do: 1. Now use the three trick chits. 2. For 'soft near', just touch the tumbler gently with the spoon. 3. For 'hard far', hit it firmly, but not hard enough to dent it. 4. Write each guess.
flow.say: Same again. Cover your ears and count to ten. Hands down. Listen. Near or far?
flow.kid: Cover your ears. Count to ten. Listen. Near or far?
flow.parent: Many children call the soft near tap 'far', and the hard far tap 'near'. In a small flat it may not work every time. If your child gets these right too, ask how they knew. Some children notice the echo in the room, and ears really do use echo. That is a good result too.

flow.do: 1. Uncover your child's eyes. 2. Show the results together. 3. Ask what they found, what they saw and why. 4. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Look at the normal rounds and the trick rounds. Which ones tricked you? Why do you think the soft tap close by sounded far away?
flow.kid: Which rounds tricked you? Why did the soft tap sound far?

check.q: In the trick round, a soft tap close by sounded far away. Why?
options: Your ears heard a soft sound, and soft sounds are usually far
check.why: Your ears tell you how loud a sound is. You guess near or far from that. Far sounds are usually soft, so a soft tap close by can trick you.

flow.think: If a loud sound can be far and a soft sound can be near, how else could you tell where a sound is?

activities.title: The Listening Window: near sounds and far sounds
activities.context: This is a quick way to start the unit. You sit by a window with your eyes shut, count the sounds you hear, and say which are near and which are far.

schedule.what: Listen with eyes shut for two minutes. Say each sound and whether it is near or far. Draw one near and one far sound.

activities.record: Fold a paper in half. On one side draw a near sound you heard, and on the other side a far sound.

setup.art: A child and a parent sitting on the floor by an open window of a flat, both with their eyes shut, the child holding up two fingers.
setup.caption: 1. Sit by the window and shut your eyes. Hold up a finger for each sound.

setup.art: A paper folded in half: on one side a drawing of a ceiling fan, on the other a tiny aeroplane in the sky.
setup.caption: 2. Draw one near sound and one far sound.

flow.do: 1. Sit with your child by a window or on the balcony. 2. Both shut your eyes for two minutes. 3. Your child holds up one finger for each new sound.
flow.say: Shut your eyes. Let's be very quiet for two minutes. Hold up a finger every time you hear a new sound.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Be very quiet. Hold up a finger for each sound.

flow.do: Open your eyes. Your child names each sound and says near or far.
flow.say: What did you hear? Was it near or far? How do you know?
flow.kid: Say each sound. Was it near or far? How do you know?

ask.q: How do you know that sound was far?
good: It was soft.
It came from down the road.
It was a small sound.

flow.parent: Most children hear several sounds in two minutes, even in a quiet flat. Do not explain yet. Just collect their reasons.

flow.do: Your child draws one near sound and one far sound.
flow.say: Draw one sound that was near, and one that was far.
flow.kid: Draw a near sound. Draw a far sound.

activities.title: Look at Your Ears: flaps, folds, covering and cupping
activities.context: In this activity you look at your own ears in a mirror and at the ears of your family. Then you cover your ears and cup your ears, and hear what changes.

materials.item: a phone playing soft music, or a radio

activities.safety: Never put a finger, a cotton bud, a pencil or anything else inside an ear. Only touch the outside.

schedule.what: Look at ears in a mirror, find the ear flap and ear hole, then cover and cup your ears while music plays.

activities.record: Draw your own ear from the mirror. Point to the ear flap and the ear hole, and a grown-up writes the names.

setup.art: A girl looking at her ear sideways in a mirror while touching the curly edge of her ear flap with one finger.
setup.caption: 1. Look at your ear in a mirror. Touch the ear flap.

setup.art: The same girl with her hands cupped behind both ears, listening to a phone on the table, smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Cover your ears, then cup them. What changes?

flow.do: 1. Your child looks at one ear in a mirror. 2. They touch the curly folds of the ear flap. 3. They find the ear hole. 4. Look at each other's ears.
flow.say: Look at your ear in the mirror. This part you can touch is the ear flap. The little opening is the ear hole. Are my ears the same shape as yours?
flow.kid: Look at your ear. Touch the ear flap. Find the ear hole.
flow.parent: Every ear has its own shape, a little like a fingerprint. Tell your child that the eardrum is deep inside, at the end of the ear hole, too far in to see.

flow.do: 1. Play soft music on a phone across the room. 2. Your child covers both ears with their hands, then lets go. 3. Then they cup their hands behind their ears.
flow.say: Cover your ears tight. What happens to the music? Now cup your hands behind your ears, like this. What happens now?
flow.kid: Cover your ears. Is the music softer? Now cup your hands behind your ears.

ask.q: What changed when you cupped your hands?
good: The music got a little louder.
My hands caught more sound.

flow.parent: Covering the ears blocks some sound. This is how we protect ears from very loud sounds like firecrackers. Cupping makes the ear flap bigger, so it catches more sound.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Which of these is a safe way to look after your ears?
flow.kid: Which is a safe way to look after your ears?

check.q: Which is a safe way to look after your ears?
options: Cover them when a sound is very loud
Clean inside them with a pencil
Put your ear right next to a loudspeaker
check.why: Covering your ears blocks some of a very loud sound. Never put anything inside your ear, and stay away from very loud speakers.

activities.title: Find the Hidden Song: louder means closer
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up hides a phone playing a soft song somewhere in the flat. You find the phone by listening, getting closer as the song gets louder.

materials.item: a phone that can play a song

schedule.what: Hide a phone playing a soft song three times. Your child finds it by listening, then hides it for the grown-up.

activities.record: Draw a map of the room with the place where the phone was hidden. Draw arrows to show the way you walked.

setup.art: A woman tucking a phone playing music under a cushion on a sofa, while a boy waits in the next room with his hands over his eyes.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides a phone playing a soft song.

setup.art: The boy walking slowly towards the sofa with one hand cupped behind his ear, and curved lines growing bigger near the cushion.
setup.caption: 2. Walk towards the sound. Louder means you are closer.

flow.do: 1. Your child waits in another room. 2. Play a song softly on a phone. 3. Hide the phone under a cushion, behind a curtain or in a basket. Never hide it in a high or unsafe place.
flow.say: I am hiding a phone that is playing a song. When I call you, find it with your ears.
flow.kid: Wait in the other room. Then find the phone with your ears.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks slowly around the room listening. 2. Ask if the song is louder or softer. 3. Do three rounds.
flow.say: Is the song louder or softer now? Then are you getting closer, or further away?
flow.kid: Walk slowly. Is it louder? Then you are getting closer.

ask.q: How did you find the phone?
good: I went where the song got louder.
When it got softer I turned back.

flow.parent: If your child finds it too fast, make the song softer. If it is too hard, make it a little louder.

flow.do: Swap. Your child hides the phone and you find it. Then ask the check question.
flow.say: Now you hide it, and I will find it with my ears.
flow.kid: Now you hide the phone. A grown-up finds it.

check.q: You walk towards the hidden phone. What happens to the song?
check.why: The closer you are to a sound, the more of it reaches your ears. So the song gets louder as you come closer.

activities.title: Move Like a Listener: elephants, crickets and frogs
activities.context: In this moving activity you act out how three animals hear. You stamp and feel the floor like an elephant, listen with your knees like a cricket, and sit still like a frog.

materials.item: a clear space on the floor

schedule.what: Act out the elephant, the cricket and the frog. Say where each animal's ears are.

activities.record: Draw one of the animals and circle where their ears are.

setup.art: A child standing still with bare feet flat on the floor while a grown-up stamps gently a few steps away.
setup.caption: 1. Be an elephant. Feel the stamp through your feet.

setup.art: A child crouching like a cricket, and a child sitting like a frog with eyes wide open.
setup.caption: 2. Be a cricket, then a frog. Where are their ears?

flow.do: 1. Your child stands barefoot, eyes shut. 2. You stamp gently on the floor a few steps away. 3. They raise a hand when they feel it.
flow.say: Elephants call their family with very low rumbles. They may feel some of them through their feet. Stand still and shut your eyes. Can you feel my stamp?
flow.kid: Be an elephant. Stand still. Shut your eyes. Can you feel the stamp?

ask.q: Where did you feel the stamp?
good: In my feet.
In my legs.

flow.parent: A gentle stamp is enough. Many children feel it in their feet before they hear it. This is a feeling activity, so no right answer.

flow.do: 1. Your child crouches like a cricket. 2. They point to their knees. 3. You hum a tune, and they creep towards you.
flow.say: A female cricket hears with ears on her front legs, just below her knees. She walks towards a singing male. Crawl to my song!
flow.kid: Be a cricket. Point to your knees. Creep towards the song.
flow.parent: A cricket's ears are small round patches on the front legs, just below the knee joint.

check.why: A cricket's ears are small patches on her front legs, just below the knee. Every animal's ears are in the right place for their own life.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits like a frog. 2. Show where a frog's eardrum is, on the side of the head behind the eye.
flow.say: A frog's eardrum is a round circle on the outside, just behind the eye. Where is your eardrum?
flow.kid: Be a frog. Where is a frog's eardrum? Where is yours?

projects.title: My Sound Map: near and far sounds over three days
projects.context: In this project you draw a map of sounds. Your home is in the middle of the page. Near sounds go close to your home, and far sounds go near the edge.

materials.item: a big sheet of paper or newspaper

schedule.what: Draw your home in the middle. Listen for two minutes in the morning. Draw each sound close or far.
Listen for two minutes in the afternoon. Add the new sounds.
Listen for two minutes in the evening. Add the new sounds. Show the map to someone.

projects.record: The finished sound map, with near sounds close to your home and far sounds near the edge.

setup.art: A big sheet of paper with a small drawing of a block of flats in the middle and three circles drawn around it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your home in the middle, with circles around it.

setup.art: The same sheet filled with small drawings: a fan and a cooker near the middle, a crow and a horn further out, an aeroplane and a train at the edge.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each sound. Near ones close, far ones at the edge.

flow.do: 1. Draw your home in the middle of the big sheet. 2. Draw three big circles around it: near, middle and far. 3. Listen together for two minutes. 4. Your child draws each sound in a circle.
flow.say: This is a map of sounds. Our home is in the middle. Listen. Where does each sound go: near, middle or far?
flow.kid: Draw your home in the middle. Listen. Draw each sound close or far.

flow.do: In the afternoon, listen again for two minutes and add the new sounds.
flow.say: It is afternoon now. Are there new sounds? Are any of the morning sounds gone?
flow.kid: Listen again. Add any new sounds to your map.
flow.wait: Do this again in the afternoon of day 2.

flow.do: In the evening of day 3, listen and add sounds. Your child shows the map to someone.
flow.say: Which sound on your map is the farthest away? How do you know?
flow.kid: Show your map. Which sound was the farthest?

check.q: On your sound map, where do you draw an aeroplane flying high in the sky?
options: Near the edge, with the far sounds
check.why: An aeroplane is far up in the sky. It is loud, so you hear it, but it belongs with the far sounds.

challenges.title: Call Everyone for Dinner Without Shouting
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Dinner is ready, and the family is in different rooms. You find a way to tell everyone, without shouting.
challenges.problem: Dinner is ready. Everyone at home is in a different room: one person is in the far bedroom, and another is on the balcony. Shouting is not allowed, because the baby next door is asleep. How can you call everyone?
constraints: Use things from home, or your own body.
materials: a small bell, if you have one
general: Walk to each room and say it in a normal voice. Going closer makes a soft sound loud enough.
Ring a small bell once. Everyone knows it means dinner, and it does not wake the baby like a shout.
Agree on a signal, like three knocks on the door, that means dinner.
creative: Roll a newspaper into a cone and speak softly through it towards each room.
Flash a torch on the wall where each person sits.
Make up a family clap: clap, clap, pause, clap means 'come and eat'.
challenges.your_turn: Choose your best idea and try it tonight. Did everyone come? Did the baby next door stay asleep?

setup.art: A floor plan of a small flat: a girl in the kitchen with a plate of food, a person reading in a far bedroom, and another on the balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Everyone is in a different room. How will you call them?

setup.art: The girl knocking three times on a door while holding a finger to her lips, and the person inside looking up and smiling.
setup.caption: 2. Try your idea. No shouting.

flow.do: Read the problem to your child.
flow.say: Dinner is ready, but the others are in far rooms. The baby next door is asleep, so no shouting. How could you call them?
flow.kid: Dinner is ready. No shouting. How will you call everyone?

good: Walk to them and tell them.
Ring a bell.
Knock on the door.

flow.do: Your child draws one or two ideas. Talk about each one.
flow.say: Draw your idea. Will the sound reach the far room? Will it wake the baby?
flow.kid: Draw your idea. Will the far room hear it?

flow.do: Try the best idea at home.
flow.say: Let's try it. I will wait in the far room.
flow.kid: Try your idea. Did the far room hear it?

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: Did it work? What would you change?
flow.kid: Did it work? What would you change?

check.q: Your voice is too soft to reach the far room. What is the simplest fix that is not shouting?
options: Walk closer to the room and speak
check.why: A sound gets softer as it travels. If you walk closer, your normal voice has less far to go, so it is loud enough.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a child's ear, and a round picture of the inside. Say the name of each part, and a grown-up writes it.
labels: the part you can see and touch
the small tunnel into the head
the thin skin at the end of the tunnel
items.why: A strong answer names all three. The ear flap catches sound, the ear hole leads in, and the eardrum shakes when sound reaches it.
items.art: A child's ear from the side, and a round zoom picture of the ear hole as a tunnel with a thin skin at its end, with three empty labels.

items.p: Draw a line from each animal to where their ears are.
pairs: Big flaps on the sides of the head
One on each side of your head
items.why: Every animal's ears are where they help that animal. A cricket's ears are on her front legs, and a frog's eardrums are on the outside of the head.
items.art: A cricket, a frog, an elephant and a child on the left, and four small pictures of ears in different places on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Is each sound near you or far away? Circle near sounds in green and far sounds in red. A grown-up reads each one.
items: A temple bell across the town
The tap running in your bathroom
A crow cawing from a tree down the road
items.why: Your clapping, your footsteps and the bathroom tap are right by you. The temple bell and the crow are far away, so they sound softer.

items.p: Plan a game to test if you can tell how far away a sound is. Draw a chair where you sit with your eyes covered, a near spot and a far spot where a grown-up taps.
items.a: A drawing of a chair with one spot close behind it and one spot far away.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the near spot one step behind the chair and the far spot across the room.
items.art: A blank box with a small chair drawn in the middle.

items.p: A sound gets softer as it travels further away.
items.why: True. The sound spreads out as it travels, so less of it reaches your ear from far away.

items.p: A loud sound is always close to you.
items.why: False. A fire engine siren far down the road is very loud. Loud sounds can be near or far.

items.p: Three of these are parts of the ear. Which one is not?
items.why: The ear flap, the ear hole and the eardrum are parts of the ear. The eyelid is part of the eye.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: tell one sound you heard at the Listening Window, and how you knew if it was near or far.
items.a: A sound the child really heard, with a reason such as 'it was loud, so I thought near' or 'it was soft, so I thought far'.
items.why: A strong answer names a real sound and gives a reason from how loud it was. It may also say a guess can be wrong.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 1, hears the vegetable seller calling in the street. The call gets louder and louder. What is the vegetable seller doing?
items.why: A sound is louder when it is closer. If the call gets louder and louder, the seller is coming closer.

items.p: Lakshmi and her friend Bornali hear a very loud clap of thunder.

views.says: That thunder was so loud. The storm must be right above our building.
Thunder is always very loud. So even loud thunder can be far away.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason. For Lakshmi: closer thunder is louder, so a very loud clap may mean the storm is near. For Bornali: thunder is so big that we hear it from far away.
items.why: Both girls are partly right. Louder thunder often means a closer storm, but thunder is so loud that even far thunder can sound big.

items.p: Draw something you can hear right now but cannot see.
items.a: A drawing of a sound-maker that is out of sight, such as a bird outside or a cooker in the kitchen.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that ears tell us about things we cannot see, even behind walls.
items.art: A blank box with a window drawn at one side.

items.p: Why do we have two ears, one on each side of the head?
opts: To hear sounds from every side and tell where they come from
So that one ear can rest
Because one ear is a spare
items.why: A sound on your left reaches your left ear a tiny bit sooner and louder. Your two ears together help you find where a sound is.

items.p: Put these in order, from the outside of your ear to the inside.
items.why: Sound is caught by the ear flap, goes down the ear hole, and reaches the eardrum at the end.

items.p: A boy called Rohan cups his hand behind his ear to hear his grandmother's soft voice. What happens to her voice? Why? Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: Her voice sounds a little louder, because his hand catches more sound and sends it into his ear.
items.why: A strong answer says the cupped hand works like a bigger ear flap.

items.p: Draw a line from each sound to the best thing to do.
pairs: A wedding loudspeaker right next to you
Move away or cover your ears
A whisper you want to hear
Come closer, or cup your ear
Cover your ears and stand far back
items.why: Very loud sounds can hurt ears, so we move away or cover them. To hear a soft sound, we come closer or catch more of it with a cupped hand.

items.p: Which sounds could trick you? Sort them into 'soft but near' and 'loud but far'.
items: A friend whispering right behind you
A fire engine siren far down the road
A watch ticking on your wrist
items.why: A soft sound close by can seem far away, and a loud sound far away can seem near. These are the sounds that can trick your ears.

items.p: Draw an elephant listening to her family far away. Draw her family small, at the other side of the page.
items.a: An elephant on one side, with tiny elephants far away on the other side, and maybe lines for the rumble between them.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a long way between them, because elephants hear their family's low rumbles from far away.

items.p: Farhan and his sister Devi are at home. Their mother stands at the kitchen door and calls 'Dinner!' in her normal voice. Farhan is near the door. Devi is in the far bedroom. Who hears the call louder?
opts: Both hear it just as loud
items.why: The call gets softer as it travels. Farhan is closer, so more of the sound reaches him.

items.p: Here is a drawing of a frog's head. Say what each part is, and a grown-up writes it.
labels: the big round circle just behind the eye
the round part at the front of the head, that sees
items.why: A frog's eardrum is on the outside of the head, just behind the eye. Ours is hidden deep inside the ear hole.
items.art: A green frog's head from the side, with an empty label pointing at the round eardrum behind the eye and another at the eye.

items.p: Babies can hear their mother's voice before they are born.
items.why: True. Babies hear inside their mother's body. A few days after birth, babies already prefer their mother's voice.

items.p: Your friend says: 'If I can't see a thing, I can't know where it is.' Shut your eyes. How could your ears show your friend another way? Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: I could shut my eyes and point to my friend when they say my name. Or I could find a hidden phone by walking to where the song gets louder.
items.why: A strong answer uses something from the unit, such as the Find the Hidden Song game or pointing to a voice, to show that ears can tell where a sound is.

videos.title: How elephants talk with sounds too low for us to hear
videos.why: Shows elephants calling each other with rumbles too low for people to hear, and how scientists found them.
videos.check: Found by search: "Mystery of Elephant Infrasounds Revealed | Animal Super Senses | BBC Earth" by BBC Earth, 3 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Why crickets sing, close up
videos.why: Close-up footage of a cricket singing to be heard by other crickets. A parent can point out that crickets hear with ears on their front legs.
videos.check: Found by search: "Why Crickets Just Won't Shut Up | Deep Look" by Deep Look, 4 minutes. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Feeling sound with Evelyn Glennie
videos.why: Evelyn Glennie is a drummer who is deaf. She plays barefoot and feels sound through her body. It shows that hearing is more than ears.
videos.check: Found by search: "Feeling Sound with Evelyn Glennie" by Evelyn Glennie, 6 minutes. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Which part of your ear can you see and touch?
quiz.why: The ear flap is the outside part with curly folds. The eardrum is deep inside, at the end of the ear hole.

opts: Deep inside, at the end of the ear hole
On the outside of your ear flap
quiz.why: The eardrum is a thin skin at the end of the ear hole. You cannot see your own, but a doctor can with a small torch.

quiz.p: A temple bell rings. Where does it sound softest?
quiz.why: A sound gets softer as it travels further away. Three streets away, only a little of the sound reaches you.

quiz.p: You walk away from a ringing phone. What happens to the sound?
quiz.why: The further you go, the softer the ring sounds, because less of the sound reaches your ears.

quiz.p: With her eyes covered, Ammu hears a very soft tap. What will she probably guess?
opts: That it is right next to her
quiz.why: We usually guess that soft sounds are far away. So a soft tap close by can trick us, as in the Near or Far test.

quiz.p: How do your ears help you guess if a sound is near or far?
opts: They hear how loud the sound is, and you guess from that
They measure the distance with the eardrum
They see where the sound is
quiz.why: Your ears hear how loud a sound is, and you guess the distance from that. The guess is usually right, but a soft sound close by can trick you.

opts: On the outside of the head, behind the eyes
quiz.why: A frog's eardrums are round circles you can see, just behind the eyes. Ours are hidden inside the ear hole.

quiz.p: Elephant families can be far apart in a big forest. Which kind of sound would carry far enough to call them?
quiz.why: Very low sounds travel a long way, even through trees. Elephants rumble so low that people can hardly hear it, but other elephants hear it from far away.

quiz.p: Your ear feels itchy inside. What should you do?
opts: Wipe only the outside, and tell a grown-up if it keeps itching
Pour water in to wash it
quiz.why: Never put anything inside your ear. Ear wax keeps the inside clean by itself. A doctor can help if it keeps itching.

quiz.p: A wedding loudspeaker is blasting right next to you. What is best for your ears?
opts: Cover your ears and move away
Put your ear on the speaker
quiz.why: Very loud sounds can hurt the inside of your ears. Covering them blocks some sound, and moving away makes it softer.

quiz.p: In the Near or Far test, why did the grown-up move only while you covered your ears and counted?
opts: So that footsteps would not tell you where they were
So that you would fall asleep
So that the tumbler would get louder
quiz.why: A fair test changes only the thing we are testing. If you heard footsteps, you would know the spot without using the tap.

applications: Ambulance sirens and train horns are made very loud, so people far away can hear them and move aside.
Some hospitals in India check a newborn baby's hearing soon after birth, so help can start early.
Hearing aids make sounds louder for people who hear less.
Workers at building sites and airports wear earmuffs to protect their ears from loud machines.
Lifeguards on beaches blow loud whistles that carry far over the noise of the waves.

spotted.text: A koel calling 'ku-oo' from a tree in Chennai on a hot summer morning, heard from inside the flat.
spotted.art: A black koel bird in a mango tree beside a block of flats, with a child at a window listening.

spotted.text: A woman selling greens calling 'Keerai! Keerai!' as she walks down a street in Madurai, getting softer as she goes.
spotted.art: A woman with a basket of green leaves on her head walking down a street of houses with kolams outside, calling out.

spotted.text: Bihu drums in Guwahati heard from many streets away before the dancers come into sight.
spotted.art: Dancers in red and cream with dhol drums at the far end of a street, and a child on a balcony in the front turning to listen.

spotted.text: A ship's horn at the port in Mumbai, heard across the harbour.
spotted.art: A big ship in a harbour with tall cranes, and people on the seafront far away turning their heads.

spotted.text: A street dog in Kolkata lifting and turning her ears towards a sound before anyone else has heard it.
spotted.art: A brown street dog sitting by a yellow taxi, ears up and turned to one side.

open_questions.why_open: In 2019, evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar after hearing a bee's buzz. Other studies found pea roots growing towards the sound of water in a pipe. More teams need to test this, and scientists argue about whether to call it hearing.

open_questions.q: How do elephants feel far-away rumbles through their feet?
open_questions.why_open: Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell found that elephants may pick up the shaking of the ground with their feet and trunks. How far away they can feel a call, and how they tell who is calling, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How can you pick out Amma's voice in a noisy room full of people?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the answer. Two ears help, and knowing a voice well helps. But how the brain picks one voice out of many is not fully known.

ask_kids: Close your eyes. What is the farthest sound you can hear right now?
Is that sound near or far? How do you know?
Which sound did you hear first this morning?
Can you point to me with your eyes shut while I talk?
If you were an elephant, who would you call from far away?
What sound would you like to hear from very far away?

jokes.j: Why did the ear go to school?
What did the left ear say to the right ear?
jokes.a: Between us, there is a brain!

jokes.j: Why are elephants so good at listening?
What did the whisper say to the shout?
Why did the cricket carry her ears on her legs?
jokes.a: So she could run towards the music!

jokes.j: Why did the elephant never need a phone?
jokes.a: She could call her family with a low rumble!

jokes.j: Why did the thunder never win at hide and seek?
jokes.a: Everyone could hear it from far away!

jokes.j: Why did the drum never win an argument?

maths.problem: In the Near or Far test, Nila got 3 out of 3 normal rounds right. In the trick rounds, she got 1 right out of 3. How many trick rounds fooled her?
maths.explain: There were 3 trick rounds, and she got 1 right. 3 take away 1 is 2. So 2 trick rounds fooled her, but no normal round did.
maths.context: This is about the Near or Far test, where a grown-up hit a tumbler near or far while you had your eyes covered.
maths.why_maths: Counting the wrong guesses in each kind of round shows which kind tricks the ears.

maths.problem: At the Listening Window, Ravi heard 5 near sounds and 3 far sounds. Did he hear more near sounds or more far sounds? How many more?
maths.explain: 5 is bigger than 3. 5 take away 3 is 2. So Ravi heard 2 more near sounds than far sounds.
maths.context: This is about the Listening Window, where you sat with your eyes shut and counted sounds.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two counts tells you whether your home is full of near sounds or far ones.

maths.problem: On her Sound Bingo board, Meenakshi made tally marks: near sounds |||| and far sounds ||. She says, 'Far sounds are rare.' Is that true everywhere?
maths.answer: Not always. She heard 4 near sounds and 2 far sounds by her window today. At another window or another time, the counts could be different.
maths.explain: 4 is twice as many as 2 here. But one window at one time is not every place. At night, when the near sounds stop, far sounds like a train are easier to hear.
maths.context: This is about the Window Sound Bingo game, where you crossed off sounds and marked them N for near or F for far.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks let you count and compare, and then ask whether one count tells the whole story.

warmup.q: Which part of your ear can you touch?

warmup.a: Deep inside, at the end of the ear hole.

warmup.q: Does a sound get louder or softer as it travels further?
Can a soft sound close by sound far away?
warmup.a: Yes. Your ears hear that it is soft, and you guess it is far.

warmup.q: Should you put a cotton bud inside your ear?

founder: ideas/by_topic/sound.md: the observation journal of the daily soundscape, used as the Sound Map project and the Listening Window; distant thunder as sound travelling, used in the Near, Middle, Far game and the story. No notebook items are mapped to this subtopic. The Level 3 hearing unit uses the quietest-sound test, the pitch test, the door test, humming with ears shut, cupping and turning ears like a cat, a model ear and ear popping, and the five senses units use smell steps, shaker pairs and pointing at a sound with one ear blocked. So this unit uses the near-or-far loudness test, the hidden song, the listening window and the animal listener moves instead. The cover-and-cup step in Look at Your Ears is the Cambridge Stage 1 Activity 6.2.
science: Katy Payne, William Langbauer and Elizabeth Marshall Thomas, 'Infrasonic calls of the Asian elephant', Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 18 (1986), from recordings at the Washington Park Zoo, Portland, in 1984.
William Langbauer and colleagues, Journal of Experimental Biology 157 (1991): elephants in Namibia responded to recorded calls played from loudspeakers far away.
Anthony DeCasper and William Fifer, 'Of human bonding: newborns prefer their mothers' voices', Science 208 (1980).
Marine Veits, Lilach Hadany and colleagues, 'Flowers respond to pollinator sound within minutes by increasing nectar sugar concentration', Ecology Letters 22 (2019).
Monica Gagliano and colleagues, 'Tuned in: plant roots use sound to locate water', Oecologia 184 (2017).
Caitlin O'Connell-Rodwell's work on elephants sensing ground vibrations, from about 2000 onwards.
Auditory distance perception relies on loudness, the ratio of direct sound to echo, and familiarity with the source: reviewed by Pavel Zahorik and colleagues, Acta Acustica 2005.

roots.context: We have looked at our ears and tested whether they can tell near from far. Now we ask what the trick taps tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: With your eyes shut, a soft tap close by can sound far away. A hard tap from across the room can sound near. Your ears hear how loud each tap is, and you guess the distance from that. So near or far is your own guess, and a guess can be fooled.
deep_truth.habit: We think we simply hear where a sound is, the way we see a cup on the table. But ears catch only the sound itself. How far away it is, we work out from how loud it is and from its echoes.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Near or Far test, the normal taps were mostly guessed right. In the trick rounds, a soft tap one step away may be called far, and a hard tap across the room may be called near.

three.who_am_i: You are a listener. Your ears catch sounds from every side, all day, and even while you sleep.
three.what_is_life: Every animal listens for what matters to them. A cricket listens for a song, and an elephant listens for her family far away.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of sounds, near and far, all the time. Each one gets softer as it travels.

roots.thread: One tap of a spoon sends sound out on every side at once. It reaches you, your family, the crow on the ledge and the neighbour next door. Each of them hears it a little louder or softer, and makes their own guess about where it came from. Everything is conscious, and each of them listens in their own way.

teachings.source: Tirukkural 411, in the chapter on listening (Kelvi)
teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar wrote that the wealth you gain through your ears is the greatest wealth of all.
teachings.link: Your ears bring you news from near and far, from behind you and from the next street, even in the dark. In the Near or Far test, your ears told you a great deal with your eyes covered.

teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, the bell of mindfulness
teachings.teaching: The Vietnamese teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught people to stop when they hear a bell, breathe, and listen to the sound until it fades away.
teachings.link: When you listen to a bell until the end, you hear it get softer and softer. You notice the moment it becomes too soft to hear. You do the same in the practice below.

science.text: Babies hear before they are born, and know their mother's voice a few days after birth.
Evening primrose flowers made sweeter nectar within minutes of hearing a bee's buzz. Whether plants hear is still argued about.

other_view.view: Hearing is something done by beings with ears and nerves. A flower changing their nectar is a response to shaking, not hearing, and calling it listening may be going too far.

practice.title: Listen until it is gone
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. I will hit this steel tumbler once, gently. Listen to the sound as long as you can. Raise your hand when you cannot hear it any more. Now take three slow breaths. Where did the sound go?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Listen to the tumbler ring. Raise your hand when it is gone. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: Which round in the Near or Far test fooled your ears? What did your ears hear, and what did you guess?
When you cannot see where a sound comes from, is knowing how far away it is a hearing or a guess?
roots.art: A child sitting cross-legged with eyes closed next to a steel tumbler, with soft curved lines spreading out from it and fading towards the edges of the picture.

how_we_found_out.story: In 1984, an American scientist named Katy Payne was watching Asian elephants at a zoo in Portland, in the United States. She stood beside their cage for hours. Now and then she felt a throbbing in the air, though she heard almost nothing. It reminded her of standing next to the biggest pipes of a church organ, which make notes so low you feel them. Katy Payne wondered if the elephants were calling to each other with sounds too low for people to hear. Nobody had yet shown that elephant families far apart used sound to keep in touch. She came back with machines that could record very low sounds. When the recordings were played faster, the low rumbles became easy to hear. She and her team showed that elephants call with deep rumbles, and that other elephants can hear them from far away. Later, in Namibia, elephants responded to calls played from loudspeakers far away.
how_we_found_out.who: Katy Payne, an American scientist, with William Langbauer and Elizabeth Marshall Thomas
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Elephant families far apart cannot keep in touch by sound.

playtest: Walked through every game, experiment, activity, project, challenge and worksheet as a parent and a Class 1 child in a flat. Fixed: the Near, Middle, Far rules and steps now agree on swapping after 7 cards and on 4 players; unchecked claims were softened (counts of sounds children hear, newborn hearing checks, the Namibia elephant distance, the month of Katy Payne's zoo visit); the confusing first big question was reworded; two stock lines in the animals card and roots were made plain. The three video entries still have no checked clip; the validator needs exactly 3, so they stay as to-do. Step minutes, chits, example results and schedules agree.
